guide.title: A yard has its own calendar.
guide.intro: A useful seasonal plan changes with growth, weather, and the condition of the ground. These are planning prompts, not a fixed treatment prescription.

notes.title: Spring · take stock
notes.text: Check for debris, bare patches, and drainage concerns before setting a routine. Discuss grass type, soil conditions, and goals before adding treatments.

notes.title: Summer · watch the conditions
notes.text: Growth and weather can change how often a lawn needs attention. Discuss watering restrictions with your local provider and avoid treating a calendar as a universal rule.

notes.title: Fall · reset the edges
notes.text: Plan for leaf collection, bed tidying, and access before wet weather. Ask whether material removal is included or arranged separately.

notes.title: Between visits
notes.text: Keep gates accessible and flag fragile areas, irrigation components, pet waste, and items in the lawn. A little preparation helps the visit go smoothly.

faq.q: What is included in a routine visit?
faq.a: This example includes mowing, trimming, edging, and clearing clippings from hard surfaces. An actual provider would confirm access, condition, and the written scope.
Weather and ground conditions can affect a visit. A real schedule should state how changes are communicated and rescheduled.

faq.q: Does a care plan include treatments?
faq.a: Not automatically. Fertilizer, pest treatment, irrigation repair, and specialist tree work need separately qualified advice and an agreed scope.
